claims.text: High-temperature reactive-gas exposure alters deformation behavior in the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy through environment-assisted oxidation or related surface reactions.
Reactive species preferentially infiltrate grain and interphase boundaries in this alloy.
Localized oxygen infiltration nucleates and grows brittle secondary phases.
Secondary phases embedded in an fcc matrix can impede dislocation glide.
Brittle secondary phases initiate microcracks that coalesce under stress into catastrophic failure.
The as-fabricated or solution-annealed Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a single-phase fcc matrix.
Exposure between approximately 800 and 1000 °C is an applicable regime for the proposed degradation mechanism.
Oxygen-enriched interfaces, precipitates, or secondary phases cause premature crack initiation and propagation.
Increasing oxygen partial pressure increases reactive-species diffusion along grain or interphase boundaries.
Reactive environments can couple oxidation to changes in phase-transformation and dislocation mechanisms in an fcc HEA.
Higher oxygen partial pressures induce abrupt local phase transformations in the target alloy.
Rapid brittle-phase formation and intergranular cracking reduce ductility.
Sudden fracture occurs after microcrack coalescence reaches a threshold.
Oxidizing exposure significantly reduces ductility relative to inert or low-oxygen exposure.
Vacuum or inert exposure at equivalent temperature and stress produces minimal phase transformation and little or no boundary cracking.
Oxygen partial pressures at or below 10^-5 atm significantly reduce or delay degradation.
Oxygen partial pressures approaching 10^-1 atm trigger extensive oxide reactions and embrittlement.
